description: We are a small group of students from ORL FL with huge goals and aspirations! Our team is full of passionate innovators, problem-solvers, and space enthusiasts uniting our skills in coding, design, and scientific storytelling for the NASA Space Apps Challenge and with our new friend Giovanni there is only great to come!
summary: We developed a web application to discover terrestrial environments that resemble extraterrestrial landscapes. This project aims to push people into the space industry by making planetary data more accessible by using satellite data already available into a application that everyday people can use. This allows people to find places that can be used to simulate similar terrestrial or extraterrestrial conditions. This can be used to map for natural resources, find similar terrain, temperature ,sunlight conditions, and other factors depending on the mission. This can help research labs find similar mineral compositions, help test equipment, help plan for drilling operations, train astronauts, teach students in stem, plan for solar installation, and so much more with new data.
details:
What it does and how it works. Terrestrial Analog Finder compares places across Earth, the Moon and Mars. The user picks an input body, clicks a location, and picks a target body. The app returns the top ten matches, each with coordinates, a picture, a similarity score and an explanation. Each site is scored on nine factors: day and night temperature, day–night swing, sunlight, slope, roughness, relative elevation, surface type, minerals, and water ice. The browser combines the factor scores as a weighted average, so the user’s weights decide how much each factor counts.

How it’s built. Python notebooks in Google Colab download open NASA and partner-agency data and build identical tables for each body. Elevation models are resampled to the same ~1 km resolution before slope and roughness are calculated, and each site is measured over the same window: about 28 km on Earth and 30 km on the Moon and Mars. Earth cells that are ocean, vegetated or urban are flagged as non-analogs. The tables are converted into equal-area tiles about 27 km across, and the site runs as a static page on GitHub Pages with no server.

Benefits and impact. Equipment teams can choose test sites for rovers, drills, solar panels and batteries before committing to field campaigns. Researchers can find new candidate sites beyond the few well-known ones. Every match lists its factor scores and shows where the comparison breaks down. Absolute mode compares real units, and relative mode compares each place’s rank within its own planet.

Tools. Python with pandas, NumPy (BSD-3), xarray, requests, pyarrow (Apache-2.0), rasterio, h5py, astropy, astropy-healpix (BSD-3), earthaccess, pyhdf, pyshp, pytest (MIT) and matplotlib (Matplotlib License), in Jupyter notebooks (BSD-3) on Google Colab; JavaScript with React, react-dom, react-router-dom, Vite, @vitejs/plugin-react, globe.gl and three.js (MIT), Leaflet (BSD-2) and react-leaflet (Hippocratic License 2.1), running the search in a Web Worker; Node.js; GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions (checkout, setup-node, upload-pages-artifact, deploy-pages; MIT) for hosting; ChatGPT.

Creativity. The tool matches across any pair of bodies, not just Moon or Mars against a fixed list of Earth sites. New mission data can be added as one more factor without rebuilding the system.

Design choices. We kept only measurements that can be taken the same way on all three bodies. Missing data is left empty rather than set to zero, and a factor with no data is dropped, with its weight shared across the remaining factors. Radiation is not scored, since no Earth site shares the Moon’s or Mars’s exposure, so the results list it as a limit. The Moon’s nights are colder than anywhere on Earth, so the scoring accounts for that difference rather than forcing a match.
